title: Real-Time Rendering of Ultra-Large and Ultra-Detailed Virtual World using Voxels
abstract: Creating full-scale interactive 3D experiences imposes three antagonistic constraints: fine detail, large worlds, and real-time frame rates. Discretizing virtual environments in hierarchical voxel grids presents some key advantages with regard to those constraints. Voxels can represent all types of geometry: they are known for volumetric content like clouds, but can just as easily be used for hard-surface objects like cars, and all the in-between world of aggregate geometries like foliage that have surfaces so complex that they are better represented by an average density field. Voxels are also easy to interpolate and average while preserving appearance, making them perfect for anti-aliased rendering and level of detail (LOD), ensuring both consistent performance and visual quality. Finally, thanks to their native spatial coherence and ordered structure, voxels can easily be ray-traced. Of course, voxels also have their drawbacks, the main one being the tremendous amount of memory they occupy if stored naively. Previous work showed that by using an octree data structure combined with a cache to dynamically stream or procedurally generate only visible voxels at the appropriate resolution, it is possible to fit voxel scenes with pixel-size detail in GPU memory and reach acceptable frame rates. However, the solution proposed at the time relied on numerous back-and-forth synchronous exchanges between CPU and GPU to manage the two dependent tasks of rendering cached data and on-demand production of new data. This caused poor GPU utilization with many intervals of starvation per frame, spikes of irregular longer frames, and more generally perfectible performance. In this thesis, we revisit this idea using modern GPU capabilities. We were able to greatly improve performance by adopting more GPU-friendly data structures and restructuring the rendering pipeline architecture to be fully GPU-driven. By letting the GPU itself dynamically schedule tasks at a micro level, GPU utilization was dramatically increased and the resulting performance was doubled. This research also led us to develop a GPU utilization profiling tool suited for dynamic thread scheduling. More generally, this journey led us to tackle the question of the real-life performance of various GPU features, and in particular GPU dynamic thread scheduling and hardware sparse textures, which we experimented with and evaluated.
